patch.value: The annotation key=value grammar has three divergent comma behaviours, two of which silently corrupt the evidence text before it is made immutable

Measured on 2026-08-03 against pm 2026.8.3 in a clean isolated sandbox workspace. The key=value CSV grammar shared by every annotation facet (files, docs, notes, learnings, test, dep) resolves an embedded comma three different ways, and two of the three change the text that is then written permanently into the immutable history stream.

Probe, one item, three adds, read back through --json:

- bare value: --add 'path=a.ts,scope=project,note=alpha, beta, gamma' records note 'alpha,beta,gamma'. The value is tokenized on commas and rejoined on a bare comma, so every separator space is lost. Silent, exit 0.
- backslash escape: --add 'path=b.ts,scope=project,note=escaped\, value' records note 'escaped\, value'. The escape is never consumed, so the recorded text carries a literal backslash that the agent did not write. Silent, exit 0.
- inner quotes: --add 'path=c.ts,scope=project,note="quoted, value"' records note 'quoted, value'. This is the only correct outcome, and it is the only one no help text mentions.

pm docs behaves identically to pm files, so this is grammar-level and not per-command.

Why this is not cosmetic. Evidence notes are the project's stated mechanism for justifying a change, and the Non-Negotiables require every code, docs or test change to be linked with an evidence note. That note is appended to an append-only history stream and hashed into the integrity chain. The chain therefore proves, correctly and permanently, that a corrupted string was recorded. Integrity verification cannot detect this because the corruption happens above the storage layer, before hashing: pm validate --check-history-drift reports ok, because nothing drifted. The record is faithful to a value that was already wrong.

The failure mode is also biased toward exactly the values that matter most. Prose evidence notes contain commas; ids, paths and enum values do not. So the grammar is lossless for the fields that would be noticed and lossy for the free text that carries the reasoning.

This is the same class as the closed finding that --add stored the flag-like token '--stdin' as literal content: the annotation parser accepts a shape it cannot faithfully represent and reports success. That one was fixed at the flag-token layer; the separator layer was not covered.

Scope is the value-parsing grammar for key=value annotation payloads only. The positional-argument lexicon has its own owner, and the flag-spelling lexicon has its own owner. This is whether a value survives the parser unchanged.

A comma inside an annotation value round-trips byte-identically through --add and the JSON read, for files, docs, notes, learnings, comments, test and dep; Exactly one documented mechanism exists for embedding a separator in a value, and the other spellings either work identically or fail loudly; A backslash escape is either consumed as an escape or rejected, never stored literally; The chosen mechanism is named in the --help text of every command that accepts the key=value grammar; A regression test asserts the round-trip for all three spellings against a sandbox workspace
pm 2026.8.3, clean sandbox workspace (PM_PATH isolated), Linux
pm files <id> --add "path=a.ts,scope=project,note=alpha, beta, gamma" then pm files <id> --json
The recorded note is the text the agent wrote: 'alpha, beta, gamma'.
The recorded note is 'alpha,beta,gamma'. The value is split on every comma and rejoined with the bare separator, so the whitespace after each comma is destroyed. Exit code is 0 and nothing warns.

author: harness:claude-code
message: Wire annotation-value grammar defect into grammar-conformance and provable-history lineage
